title: Fat Cat McRee's live Manassas albums and Tommy Gwaltney's group
summary: How live festival recordings get taped and released, with musicians Fat Cat brings in, many from Blues Alley.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x:
Now the next album we
come to is one of a series that you done for Pat Cat
Johnson McRee on his label, 'The Fat Cat Jazz Label,'
which he publishes from Manassas, Virginia.
And it contains, basically, three
kinds of material. The first was recorded in July
of '69 -- and I'll let you talk about that.
The other two sessions are both from
live performances at the Manassas jazz festival in
either 1970 or in '72.
Can you tell us about the 1969 sides
on this album?

You know, when you do
the Manassas jazz festival, you don't work with the
same group of musicians the whole time you're there.
It's a three-day affair, you know. And
you perform at least twice -- two concerts a day and

then the final on, like Sunday. But you're not working with the same group all the time.
So, when these things are -- when you're performing, they're being taped at the same time.
But I think that what Fat Cat does is, after he gets all his material together that's on tape, then he edits.
And he puts stuff out that he -- which is probably the best that he has.

Of course, you know when you're recording live, there can be some little blips or things like that, that may not turn out too good, especially when you're before a large audience and you're doing so much work in such a short time.
These -- most of these things are with musicians that Fat Cat brings in from out of town -- guys that you probably don't hear about all the time.
Tommy Gwaltney was the owner of Blues Alley, and clarinetist and played vibraphones. So he always shows up.
And when I work at Blues Alley on occasion --

Blues Alley is a jazz club in Washington, D.C.?

Right. It would be Tommy's group. So when I do the jazz festival, I always like to work with Tommy and Johnny Eaton, and, of course, Bill Goodall, and whatever drummer is available. So -- Steve Jordan is a very good guitarist. He's from one of the big bands in the old era. He's a guitarist and he sings. But he's very good and he's got a very good sense of rhythm. Bertell Knox is a local drummer. I think he was out with Ella on tour for a long time. He's a very good man on brushes. He showed up, and it's very good to work with someone like that. Billy Taylor, the bass player, is -- well was, he passed a couple of years ago -- the son of another Billy Taylor who was a bass man who was around for years. You may know that. These guys were the

Four of these selections were made
at the club for purposes of submitting to the State

We were hoping that we'd be able
to do a tour for the state department. But it didn't
come throught for some reason or other.
